title: ORDER BY Without an Index Adds a Sort
description: An ORDER BY on an unindexed column adds an expensive Sort; an index that stores rows in that order removes it.
narrative:
## Scenario
`SELECT TOP (100) ProductId, Price FROM Products ORDER BY Price` returns the 100 cheapest products. The plan has an expensive **Sort** operator even though you only want 100 rows.

## Why it's slow
Nothing stores the rows in `Price` order, so to find the smallest 100 SQL Server must **sort all 200k rows** at run time (a *Top N Sort*). Sorting is CPU- and memory-heavy and, on bigger inputs, can spill to tempdb.

## What to look for
- A **Sort** (often *Top N Sort*) operator, typically the most expensive node in the plan.

## The concept
An index is a **pre-sorted** structure. With an index on `Price`, the rows are already in order, so the optimizer just reads the first 100 from the index and skips the Sort entirely. Indexes don't only speed up `WHERE` — they also satisfy `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY`, `TOP`, and `MIN`/`MAX` by providing order for free.
startingQuery: SELECT TOP (100) ProductId, Price FROM Products ORDER BY Price;
hints: The Sort operator is doing the work — where would pre-sorted rows come from?
There is no index on Price, so all 200k rows are sorted at run time.
Create an index: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Products_Price ON Products(Price);
